1.title: Programming Concepts for Data Engineering
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Programming Concepts for Data Engineering. This module covers the task statement: apply programming concepts. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Optimize code to cut runtime in ingestion and transformation. Configure Lambda for concurrency, memory, storage and performance. Pick languages and frameworks for data engineering. Apply software engineering practices: version control, testing, logging, monitoring. Deploy with infrastructure as code: CloudFormation, C D K (Cloud Development Kit) and A W S S A M (Serverless Application Model). Describe C I (continuous integration) or C D (continuous delivery) for data pipelines, distributed computing, and data structures and algorithms.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Speeds Up Its Nightly Job
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Speeds Up Its Nightly Job. The nightly transform takes six hours and the window is four. It loops over rows one by one, calls an A P I per record and writes thousands of tiny files. Your job: make it fit the window without more servers.

1.title: Optimizing Code and Runtime
1.text: Optimizing Code and Runtime. Row-by-row loops. Vectorized or set-based operations (S Q L, DataFrames) instead of per-record code. Reading too much data. Filter early (push-down predicates), read only needed columns, partition pruning, columnar formats. Expensive shuffles. Broadcast the small side of a join, filter before joining, partition on the join key. Repeated work. Cache reused data; do expensive setup once (see Lambda init code below). One call per record. Batch requests (BatchWriteItem, PutRecords, bulk copy), reuse connections. Tiny output files. Coalesce or compact to larger files. Sequential work that is independent. Parallelize (more partitions, workers, concurrent tasks).

1.title: Optimizing Code and Runtime, continued
1.text: Optimizing Code and Runtime, continued. Guessing. Measure first: CloudWatch metrics, Spark U I, profilers. Exam tip: The fix for slow E T L (extract, transform, load) is usually less data read, set-based processing, parallelism, and fewer larger files, not a bigger instance by default.

1.title: Lambda Concurrency and Performance
1.text: Lambda Concurrency and Performance. Memory (one hundred twenty-eight megabytes to ten thousand two hundred forty megabytes). Also sets C P U share: more memory means more C P U and often a faster, sometimes cheaper run. Timeout. Up to fifteen minutes per invocation. Reserved concurrency. Guarantees and caps a function's concurrent executions: protects critical functions and limits load on a downstream database; no extra charge; setting zero stops the function. Provisioned concurrency. Pre-initialized environments to remove cold starts; extra charge; helps interactive (latency-sensitive) workloads, rarely needed for pipelines.

1.title: Lambda Concurrency and Performance, continued
1.text: Lambda Concurrency and Performance, continued. Account concurrency. Default one thousand concurrent executions per Region (can be raised); you can reserve up to the unreserved amount minus one hundred. Ephemeral storage ( or tmp). five hundred twelve megabytes to ten thousand two hundred forty megabytes, per execution environment, encrypted at rest: scratch space for E T L, large objects, models. Event source mapping. Batch size, batching window, parallelization factor, error handling for streams and queues (Module two). Architecture. Arm (Graviton) often cheaper and faster than x eighty-six for the same work. Estimate concurrency equals average requests per second times average duration in seconds.

1.title: Lambda Concurrency and Performance, continued
1.text: Lambda Concurrency and Performance, continued. Init code outside the handler (S D K clients, database connections, loaded models) runs once per environment and is reused, which reduces latency and cost. Databases: many concurrent functions open many connections: limit with reserved concurrency or use R D S (Relational Database Service) Proxy to pool them. Failure handling: destinations or a dead-letter queue for asynchronous invocations. Layers package shared libraries; container images (up to ten gigabytes) hold large dependencies.

1.title: Mounting storage in Lambda
1.text: Mounting storage in Lambda. or tmp ephemeral storage: temporary, per execution environment. Amazon E F S (Elastic File System): mount a shared, persistent file system (the function must be in a V P C (Virtual Private Cloud); use an access point; path such as or mnt or data): for large shared files, libraries or models. Amazon S three Files: a newer option that mounts an S three bucket as a file system (a function uses either E F S or S three Files, not both). Do not mount to store results you need forever: write to S three or a database. Exam tip: "Lambda must read a large shared model or reference file on every invocation" to mount Amazon E F S (or load once into or tmp at init). "A function overloads the database with connections" to reserved concurrency and R D S Proxy. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: Languages and frameworks
1.text: Languages and frameworks. Python. PySpark and Glue scripts, boto three (A W S S D K (software development kit)), pandas, Lambda, Airflow D A G s (directed acyclic graph). S Q L. Athena, Redshift, Spark S Q L, transformations and views: the common language of data. Scala. Native language of Apache Spark; Glue and E M R (Elastic MapReduce) jobs. Java. Kafka and Flink applications, Lambda, Hadoop. R. Statistics and analysis (E M R, SageMaker notebooks). Bash or PowerShell. Scripting and automation (A W S C L I (command line interface), A W S Tools for PowerShell).

1.title: Practices
1.text: Practices. Version control (Git). All code and infrastructure templates in Git; branches, pull requests, reviews. Testing. Unit tests for functions, integration tests on sample data, data tests (row counts, nulls, schema), regression checks. Logging. Structured logs with job, run and record identifiers; send to CloudWatch Logs. Monitoring. Metrics and alarms on runtime, failures, lag, data volume. Configuration and secrets. Parameters outside the code; secrets in Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store. Environments. Separate dev, test and prod with the same templates. Modularity and idempotency. Small reusable functions; re-runnable jobs. Exam tip: "Make the pipeline repeatable and reviewable" to Git for code and IaC templates plus automated tests in a pipeline.

1.title: Infrastructure as Code
1.text: Infrastructure as Code. The figure shows this: Infrastructure as code options: CloudFormation templates, A W S C D K programs and A W S S A M templates all end as CloudFormation stacks.

1.title: Infrastructure as Code, continued
1.text: Infrastructure as Code, continued. A W S CloudFormation. What it is: Declarative templates (Y A M L or Jason) that create a stack of resources. Pick it when: You need repeatable, reviewable infrastructure for any A W S resource. A W S C D K (Cloud Development Kit). What it is: Define infrastructure in a programming language (Python, TypeScript, Java and more); it synthesizes to CloudFormation. Pick it when: You want loops, functions, classes and reuse (constructs) for infrastructure. A W S S A M (Serverless Application Model). What it is: Shorthand extension of CloudFormation for serverless (Transform: A W S::Serverless-two thousand sixteen to ten to thirty-one) plus the S A M C L I. Pick it when: Lambda, A P I Gateway, DynamoDB, Step Functions pipelines.

1.title: CloudFormation essentials
1.text: CloudFormation essentials. A template describes resources; a stack is the deployed instance; change sets preview updates; drift detection finds manual changes; StackSets deploy to many accounts and Regions. Deployments are repeatable: the same template builds dev, test and prod. Rollback on failure keeps the stack consistent.

1.title: AWS SAM essentials
1.text: A W S S A M essentials. Resource types: A W S::Serverless::Function,::Api,::HttpApi,::SimpleTable (DynamoDB),::StateMachine (Step Functions) and more, expanded to CloudFormation at deploy time. S A M C L I: sam init, sam build, sam local invoke (test locally), sam deploy, sam sync (fast sync of local changes). Connectors generate the I A M (Identity and Access Management) permissions between resources. Exam tip: "Package and deploy a Lambda plus Step Functions plus DynamoDB pipeline with the least template code" to A W S S A M. "Define infrastructure with a programming language" to A W S C D K. "Repeatable deployment of any resources from a template" to CloudFormation.

2.title: CI/CD for Data Pipelines
2.text: C I C D for Data Pipelines. The figure shows this: A C I C D pipeline for data work: source control, build and test, deploy to test, approval, deploy to production, orchestrated by A W S CodePipeline. Continuous integration (C I): every change is built and tested automatically (unit tests, data tests, template validation). Continuous delivery or deployment (C D): tested changes are released automatically (delivery may add a manual approval before production).

2.title: CI/CD for Data Pipelines, continued
2.text: C I C D for Data Pipelines, continued. A W S services: A W S CodePipeline (orchestrates the stages), A W S CodeBuild (builds and runs tests), A W S CodeDeploy (deploys to Lambda, E C two (Elastic Compute Cloud), E C S (Elastic Container Service) with canary, linear or all-at-once shifts and rollback), CloudFormation (deploys the infrastructure). Source: Git hosts such as GitHub or GitLab, S three or E C R (A W S CodeCommit is no longer on the in-scope list). Data-pipeline specifics: test transformations on a small sample dataset, deploy Glue scripts to S three and update job definitions, promote the same artifact from test to production, roll back with the previous version. Exam tip: "Automatically test and deploy changes to Glue jobs and Step Functions on every commit" to CodePipeline with CodeBuild (tests) and CloudFormation or S A M (deploy).

2.title: Distributed computing
2.text: Distributed computing. Distributed computing splits data and work across many machines that cooperate, so a job scales out beyond one machine and tolerates node failures. Spark: a driver plans the job; executors run tasks on partitions of the data; a shuffle moves data between executors (expensive); lazy evaluation builds a plan first. MapReduce idea: map (process pieces in parallel) then reduce (combine); H D F S (Hadoop Distributed File System) stores blocks across nodes. Trade-offs: scale out (more nodes) versus scale up (bigger node); data locality; network cost of shuffles; skew. Services: E M R, Glue (Spark), Athena, Redshift (M P P), Kinesis shards, M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) partitions.

2.title: Data structures and algorithms
2.text: Data structures and algorithms. The figure shows this: A graph has nodes joined by edges and may contain loops; a tree is a connected graph with a root and no loops.

2.title: Data structures and algorithms, continued
2.text: Data structures and algorithms, continued. Graph. What it is: Nodes joined by edges (directed or not, loops allowed). Where you meet it: Amazon Neptune (graph database), data lineage, pipeline dependencies (D A G s), relationships (customers and shipments). Tree. What it is: A graph with a root, parents and children and no cycles. Where you meet it: Hierarchies (organization, categories), B-tree indexes in databases, partition prefixes. Hash table. What it is: Key to value by a hash function. Where you meet it: Partition keys (DynamoDB, Kinesis, Kafka), hash joins. Queue or stack. What it is: First in first out or last in first out. Where you meet it: S Q S (Simple Queue Service), buffering streams. Sorted structures. What it is: Ordered data enables binary search. Where you meet it: Sort keys, sorted columnar files.

2.title: Data structures and algorithms, continued
2.text: Data structures and algorithms, continued. Traversal visits nodes: breadth-first (level by level) and depth-first (follow a path deep first); shortest path finds the cheapest route between nodes. Complexity (Big O) describes how work grows with data size: O(one) constant (hash lookup), O(log n) (index or binary search), O(n) (full scan), O(n log n) (sorting): indexes and partitioning turn scans into lookups. Exam tip: "Model highly connected data (who is related to whom, lineage, recommendations)" to a graph and Amazon Neptune. "Look up by key fast at any size" to a hash-partitioned store such as DynamoDB.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Optimize code: Set-based, parallel, push-down filters, columnar, batch calls, fewer larger files, measure first. Lambda: one hundred twenty-eight to ten thousand two hundred forty megabytes memory (C P U scales); fifteen min. Languages: Python, S Q L, Scala (Spark), Java (Kafka or Flink), R, Bash, PowerShell. Practices: Git, tests (unit, integration, data), logging, monitoring, secrets outside code, dev or test or prod. IaC: CloudFormation (templates, stacks, change sets, drift), C D K (code to CloudFormation), S A M (serverless shorthand, sam build or deploy or local). C I C D: CodePipeline orchestrates, CodeBuild tests, CodeDeploy releases (canary or linear), CloudFormation or S A M deploys. Distributed computing: Split data and work across nodes; Spark driver or executors or partitions or shuffle; scale out; skew. Structures: Graph (Neptune, lineage, D A G s), tree (hierarchies, B-trees), hash (partition keys), queue (S Q S).

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A nightly transformation loops over millions of rows and calls an external A P I once per row, so it misses its window. Which change helps M O S T? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Batching calls and using set-based parallel processing removes per-record overhead. A bigger server does not remove the serial work.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Select two. A Lambda function reading from a stream overwhelms a relational database with connections during spikes. Which two actions reduce the problem? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Reserved concurrency limits how many functions run at once, and R D S Proxy pools connections. More memory or provisioned concurrency does not reduce connections.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A team wants to define a pipeline made of Lambda functions, a Step Functions state machine and a DynamoDB table with the least template code, and test the functions locally. Which tool should they use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A W S S A M is a CloudFormation extension with shorthand for serverless resources and a C L I for local testing and deployment.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Developers want to define cloud infrastructure using loops and reusable classes in Python, and still deploy through CloudFormation. Which tool fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The A W S C D K lets you define infrastructure in a programming language and synthesizes CloudFormation templates.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A Lambda function must load a three gigabytes reference file on every invocation and share it across many functions. Which approach is B E S T? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. E F S provides a shared, persistent file system that Lambda can mount; deployment packages and event payloads have size limits.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. An analyst needs to represent customers, shipments and the relationships between them for queries such as "which customers share a delivery address?" Which data structure and service fit best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Highly connected data is modeled as a graph, and Amazon Neptune is the managed graph database.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: D. Question two: A and E. Question three: C. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
